This study presents a precise analytical investigation of two quasiparticle excitations within the fractional quantum Hall effect, specifically focusing on the $\nu=1/3$ state. By employing the exact analytical framework of the Laughlin wave function, we derive the energy of these quasiparticles as a function of their separation distance. Our findings indicate that the energy of a quasiparticle pair exhibits a minimum at a specific, non-zero separation, a result that contrasts with the conventional assumption of a minimum occurring at zero separation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the energy of a single quasiparticle decreases monotonically as the system size increases, a behavior that aligns with established theoretical expectations.

This study examines a variational inequality modeling the motion of a glacier sliding over a rough bedrock, where the frictional resistance is defined by a power-law function of the sliding velocity. The analysis focuses on the finite element approximation of this problem, specifically employing a nonconforming $P_1$ element for the velocity field and a piecewise constant element for the Lagrange multiplier representing the frictional stress. The work establishes the existence and uniqueness of both the continuous and discrete solutions, along with the convergence of the discrete solution toward the continuous one. Furthermore, the authors derive an a priori error estimate for the velocity field.

Galactic outflows are a critical component of star formation regulation, yet their impact on the star formation efficiency (SFE) of individual star-forming regions remains unclear. This study utilizes the DUVET instrument to conduct spatially resolved observations of the starbursting disk galaxy NGC 253, analyzing the relationship between outflows and SFE. We measured the SFE within 100 pc regions using 24 μm flux and Hα emission, while determining outflow velocities and mass loading factors (η) through CO(2-1) and CO(3-2) line profiles. Our results indicate that outflows are ubiquitous in NGC 253, with 80% of star-forming regions exhibiting outflow signatures. Furthermore, we identified a significant correlation between SFE and η, suggesting that outflows play a pivotal role in governing star formation.

This study examines the triangular flow $v_3$ in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV using the multiphase transport (AMPT) model. We analyze the dependence of $v_3$ on centrality, transverse momentum, and system size, comparing our results with experimental data from the STAR collaboration. Additionally, we investigate the influence of the initial state on $v_3$ by varying the initial energy density and the initial transverse profile.

This paper introduces a new robotic structure designed to enable simultaneous manipulation of multiple objects. The proposed mechanism consists of a single actuator driving a linkage system that connects to two end-effectors. The design is derived from a four-bar linkage, which is modified by replacing one link with a two-degree-of-freedom end-effector. The resulting structure is compact, lightweight, and capable of handling various object sizes. The study details the design methodology, kinematic analysis, and control strategies. The system's performance is validated through experiments involving the concurrent manipulation of two objects.

This study investigates whether pre-training on monocular depth estimation yields better results for semantic segmentation than pre-training on classification. We evaluate these approaches using the Cityscapes dataset, which is a standard benchmark for semantic segmentation. Our findings indicate that depth-based pre-training outperforms classification-based pre-training, achieving a 1.5% improvement in mean Intersection over Union (mIoU). Furthermore, we demonstrate that the depth pre-training model can be effectively utilized for downstream tasks such as instance segmentation and object detection.

This paper establishes a new Bohr radius for the class of starlike log-harmonic functions, improving upon the result by Ali et al. (2014). Additionally, we derive a Bohr radius for the class of log-harmonic functions, which is larger than the one found by Wu et al. (2016).

This paper addresses the challenge of estimating the Kendall's tau correlation coefficient for a bivariate copula $C$ based on a sample of $n$ observations. We introduce a novel, effective method for deriving the asymptotic variance of the resulting estimator. This approach is demonstrated through its application to the Clayton copula, where we derive the asymptotic distribution of the proposed estimator.

This paper introduces a collaborative framework designed to enable privacy-preserving edge cognition within automotive networks. The proposed system leverages a collaborative neural network (CNN) to facilitate the training of a shared model across multiple vehicles, ensuring that sensitive data remains secure. To address the challenges of network heterogeneity and the dynamic nature of vehicle connectivity, the study presents a novel collaborative structure that integrates a vehicular edge computing (VEC) network with a vehicular ad hoc network (VANET). This architecture allows vehicles to dynamically select the most suitable edge computing nodes for training tasks. Furthermore, the paper outlines a specific protocol for the collaborative training process and evaluates the system's performance through extensive simulations.

This study examines a Holling-Tanner predator-prey model incorporating a significant Allee effect within the prey population. The analysis focuses on the system's dynamics, specifically the stability of its equilibria and the occurrence of Hopf bifurcations. Furthermore, the paper derives the conditions for the existence of periodic solutions and investigates the influence of time delays on the system's stability.

This paper investigates the linear iteration limit of the aspect pivot simplex technique, a variant of the standard pivot simplex method. We demonstrate that this technique exhibits a linear iteration limit, a property that is not shared by the standard pivot simplex method.

This paper investigates the first NK_1 group of a specific type of ring defined by Bak, which is a subring of a matrix ring over a commutative ring. We establish that this NK_1 group is trivial under certain conditions.

We analyze the $t\bar{t}j$ process within the context of the Standard Model, incorporating off-shell effects via the $WW$ propagator. This study investigates the efficacy of Vision Transformers (ViTs) in zero-shot face countermeasure detection, a domain where ViTs have recently demonstrated superior performance compared to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). We evaluate ViTs against established CNN architectures using the CASIA-WebFace dataset, which includes various countermeasure types such as glasses, masks, and hats. Our findings indicate that ViTs achieve a 1.5% to 2% increase in accuracy over the best-performing CNNs. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of data augmentation and data balancing on model performance.

This paper introduces a self-driving system that leverages deep reinforcement learning to navigate complex, real-world driving scenarios. The system's architecture comprises three primary modules: a perception module utilizing a deep neural network to extract features from sensor data, a decision-making module employing a deep reinforcement learning agent to determine actions, and a control module responsible for executing those decisions. The system was trained using a simulator that generates realistic driving environments and rewards based on performance metrics. Experimental results demonstrate that the system achieves superior performance compared to traditional rule-based approaches, exhibiting robustness against various disturbances and maintaining stable operation under diverse conditions.

Parallel asynchronous evolutionary algorithms are highly effective for solving multi-objective optimization problems, yet they face a significant challenge: the evaluation time bias. This bias arises because solutions with shorter evaluation times are more likely to be selected, skewing the process toward these faster candidates. This paper introduces a new parent selection method designed to mitigate such bias. The proposed approach prioritizes solutions based on their frequency of selection, ensuring that the likelihood of being chosen is proportional to how often a solution has been selected previously. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this frequency-based strategy effectively reduces evaluation time bias. Furthermore, the method is integrated into the well-known NSGA-II algorithm to create a new variant called FNSGA-II. Empirical results confirm that FNSGA-II outperforms the standard NSGA-II in terms of both solution quality and computational efficiency.

We present the validation of OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb, a 4.5 Earth-mass exoplanet orbiting a 0.35 solar-mass M-dwarf star. This discovery was made possible through a combination of high-resolution adaptive optics imaging from the Keck Observatory and precise photometric monitoring by the OGLE survey. The planet resides at a projected separation of 0.62 AU from its host star, resulting in an equilibrium temperature of 170 K.

This study examines the depolarization of polarized neutrons within the heavy-fermion compound CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ across the entire composition range. We identify a depolarization mechanism driven by ferromagnetic fluctuations, which is most pronounced in samples with rhodium concentrations of $x \leq 0.2$. Additionally, we observe a depolarization effect attributed to spin immobilization, which becomes significant at $x \geq 0.2$.

We present a high-resolution 21 cm survey of the massive star-forming region G176.51+00.20, utilizing the Green Bank Telescope to map the molecular cloud's neutral hydrogen (HI) distribution. Our observations reveal a complex structure characterized by a prominent, dense HI ridge and a less dense, extended ridge. The dense ridge exhibits a significant self-emission component, which we attribute to the narrow-line HI self-emission (HI-HNSE) phenomenon. This emission arises from the interaction between the dense ridge and the extended ridge, where the extended ridge's neutral hydrogen acts as a scattering medium. We further identify a distinct, compact HI ridge situated between the two main ridges, which we interpret as a dense, self-emitting structure. The study concludes that the HI-HNSE mechanism is a viable method for detecting and characterizing dense, self-emitting neutral hydrogen structures within massive star-forming regions.

This study examines $\beta$-transitions in the context of the nuclear shell model, specifically focusing on the $^{14}$C nucleus. We demonstrate that the intermediate $\beta$-transitions observed in $^{14}$C can be effectively described as greedy $\beta$-transfers involving a gap. This approach utilizes a simplified model that incorporates only the dominant two-body matrix elements.

This study evaluates the efficacy of various domain migration techniques for transferring deep neural networks from source to target domains, specifically focusing on image classification tasks. We examine three distinct approaches: (1) unsupervised domain adaptation, (2) semi-supervised domain adaptation, and (3) transfer learning. Our analysis includes a comparative assessment of these methods across multiple datasets and benchmarks.
This paper presents an algorithm to enumerate arcs in $\mathbb F_q^2$ for any prime power $q$. The algorithm runs in $O(q^2)$ time and generates arcs in lexicographical order.
This paper presents a demonstration without words, featuring triangles within a geometric grid.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a dominant approach for addressing graph-based machine learning challenges. However, their training and inference processes are computationally expensive, particularly when dealing with large-scale graphs. To address this, we introduce a parameterized GNN interpreter that enables the efficient training and inference of GNNs on massive datasets. Our approach involves converting GNNs into parameterized programs, which are then executed using a graph-aware interpreter. This method allows for the direct training of GNNs by leveraging gradient descent on the underlying program parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this parameterized program can be efficiently compiled into a standard GNN architecture. Experimental results indicate that our method achieves comparable accuracy to existing GNN models while significantly reducing both training time and memory consumption.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the RXCJ0232.2-4420 cluster, a massive system with a mass of approximately $10^{15} M_{\odot}$, utilizing data from the XMM-Newton observatory. Our investigation reveals a complex internal structure characterized by multiple substructures, including a dominant central galaxy group and several smaller, distinct clumps. By examining the spatial distribution of these substructures alongside their X-ray emission profiles, we infer that the cluster's formation history is marked by significant mergers and accretion events. These findings underscore the critical role of substructure in shaping the evolution of massive clusters like RXCJ0232.2-4420.

The Legendre Memory Unit (LMU) is a memory-based recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture that has demonstrated superior performance in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, LMUs are computationally intensive, making their training prohibitively expensive for large-scale datasets. This paper introduces a parallelized training algorithm for LMUs that significantly accelerates the process. We evaluate this method on the Penn Treebank (PTB) dataset, achieving a 10-fold speedup with only a negligible impact on model performance.

Weakly-interacting particles are a primary focus of contemporary particle physics, as they may account for dark matter and the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe. This review examines the current status of experimental searches for these particles, with a specific emphasis on the most recent findings from the LHC.

We introduce a labeling game where participants assign labels to items, with the payoff for each player contingent upon the labels they provide and the subsequent labels assigned by others. This study examines the evolution of labeling strategies among players who migrate between two distinct groups. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the system converges to a state where both groups employ identical, linguistically consistent strategies. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of varying the migration rate on the system's convergence speed.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are increasingly utilized to solve partial differential equations (PDEs) across various scientific and engineering disciplines. However, PINNs face significant challenges, including slow convergence and poor performance when dealing with high-dimensional problems. This study investigates the spectral bias inherent in PINNs, revealing that it disproportionately affects the accuracy of solutions in high-dimensional settings. To mitigate this spectral bias, we propose a momentum-based optimization strategy. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach significantly accelerates convergence and markedly enhances solution accuracy.

This study examines the stability of a system comprising two coupled wave equations, where Kelvin-Voigt damping is applied to one equation and the coupling is achieved through a transmission condition at the interface. The analysis demonstrates that the system achieves exponential stability when the damping is localized within the entire domain, whereas it exhibits polynomial stability when the damping is confined to a subdomain.

Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) is a prominent approach for addressing complex tasks by decomposing them into subgoals, yet it often struggles with the "credit assignment problem" when determining which agent should execute specific subgoals. This paper introduces a novel HRL framework that leverages inductive logic programming (ILP) to generate interpretable, logic-based rules for assigning these subgoals. By utilizing ILP, the system derives a rule set that explains the rationale behind each subgoal assignment, thereby enhancing the model's transparency. Furthermore, the framework employs a model-based RL algorithm to learn the underlying dynamics of the environment, which facilitates more efficient learning. Empirical results demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms existing HRL approaches in both learning speed and final performance.

We introduce a quantum compression-based optical asymmetry that is highly sensitive to the nonlinear coefficient of a medium. This effect is demonstrated by analyzing the evolution of a quantum compressed state as it propagates through a Kerr medium. The resulting asymmetry is quantified by the difference in the variances of the quadrature components, which are defined by the nonlinear coefficient and the initial quantum compression strength. The study further examines the influence of the initial state's squeezing parameter on this asymmetry. Additionally, the asymmetry is shown to be extremely responsive to the nonlinear coefficient, exhibiting a sensitivity that surpasses that of standard quantum states.

This paper examines the minimax approximation of the sum of $n$ translates of a function $f$ by polynomials of degree at most $n-1$, specifically within the context of the space $C[a,b]$. We establish a Fenton-type theorem that provides a necessary and sufficient condition for a function $f$ to possess a best approximation of degree $n-1$ in this setting.

We present a new experimental search for spin-dependent dark matter interactions with $^6$Li, utilizing a 100-day data collection from the XENON1T detector. The analysis leverages the unique nuclear properties of $^6$Li, which features a large spin of $I=1$ and a significant neutron-proton spin asymmetry. Our results establish the most stringent limits to date on spin-dependent dark matter-nucleon cross-sections for $^6$Li, surpassing previous constraints by factors of 2 to 10.

Blind image restoration (BIR) is a critical task in computer vision, yet it remains challenging due to the lack of knowledge regarding the degradation process. This paper introduces a novel BIR framework based on kernel mixture (KM), which models the degradation kernel as a weighted combination of multiple basis kernels. By employing a variational inference approach, we derive a closed-form solution for the kernel weights and develop an efficient iterative algorithm to estimate the kernel parameters. Furthermore, we propose a new image prior that integrates both local and global information to enhance restoration quality. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This paper introduces a new class of nonuniform associativity conditions for the tensor product of two associative algebras. We demonstrate that these conditions are equivalent to a corresponding nonuniform version of the associative Yang-Baxter equation. Furthermore, we establish that the corresponding double construction yields a nonuniform pre-Lie bialgebra, which is itself equivalent to a nonuniform version of a Lie bialgebra.

This paper introduces Natural Reasoning, a formalism designed to validate programs based on natural language specifications. It extends Hoare logic by incorporating a natural language component that represents program specifications. We define a natural language fragment capable of expressing preconditions, postconditions, and invariants, and we establish a sound and complete proof system for verifying programs against these specifications. Furthermore, we present a decision procedure for determining the satisfiability of our natural language formulas.

Canopus is a distributed ledger protocol that achieves Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) by leveraging the principles of Paxos. It is designed to be resilient to network failures, ensuring that the system remains operational even when nodes disconnect. However, Canopus does not currently address scenarios where nodes fail in a Byzantine manner. This paper introduces RCanopus, an extension of Canopus that ensures Byzantine fault tolerance while maintaining the original system's robustness against network disruptions.

This study examines the bending modulus of a membrane composed of a 1:1 mixture of DPPC and cholesterol, utilizing the coarse-grained Martini force field. We conducted extensive simulations of a single bilayer, varying the system size from 128 to 1024 lipids, and analyzed the bending modulus by examining the membrane's undulations. Our findings indicate that the bending modulus is independent of system size, provided the dimensions exceed a specific threshold. Furthermore, we determined the bending modulus to be 12.5 ± 0.5 kBT, a value that aligns well with experimental data.

We present a loop quantum gravitational framework derived from the ADM Hamiltonian, which is expressed as a sum of two components: a Hamiltonian constraint and a diffeomorphism constraint. This formulation is developed within a canonical framework utilizing a specific set of variables, including the Ashtekar-Barbero connection, the densitized triad, and the extrinsic curvature.

The Pierre Auger Observatory, a facility dedicated to studying ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs), has been operational since 2004. This document serves as a comprehensive register of all UHECRs detected during Phase I of the observatory's operation, spanning from 2004 to 2010. The register includes 1,000 events with energies exceeding $10^{18}$ eV, 1,000 events above $10^{19}$ eV, and 1,000 events above $10^{20}$ eV. The data presented here is intended to facilitate future research and analysis.

Deep learning has become a standard for object detection, yet it struggles to quantify uncertainty in its predictions. This paper introduces a Bayesian approach to assess uncertainty in deep detectors, utilizing a novel Bayesian architecture that maintains the same inference speed as conventional models. We demonstrate that this method effectively estimates uncertainty in both object localization and classification. Furthermore, we show that the proposed framework can be integrated into existing detectors with minimal performance degradation.

This study introduces a novel approach to traffic prediction that leverages traffic flow snippets, which are defined as short sequences of traffic flow data. We propose a new traffic prediction model that utilizes a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to extract features from these snippets and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to forecast future traffic flow. The model is evaluated using the Caltech 100 dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods.

This paper introduces a novel category of "gray categories," which extends the concept of 2-categories by allowing 2-morphisms to be either "white" or "black." We demonstrate that the coherence theorem for 2-categories holds equally for gray categories. Furthermore, we establish a coherence theorem for a specific class of "gray categories with involution," which are defined by an anti-involution mapping white 2-morphisms to black ones and vice versa. Finally, we provide a proof that any diagram within a gray category with involution can be reduced to a canonical form, provided the diagram commutes in the underlying gray category.

This study presents a new approach to hippocampus segmentation in MRI scans, specifically targeting Alzheimer's disease and epilepsy research. The proposed method utilizes a multi-convolutional neural network architecture to segment the hippocampus into its distinct anatomical subfields. The model is trained on a dataset of 100 T1-weighted MRI images, each annotated with 10 corresponding subfield masks. The results demonstrate that the method achieves a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.89 for the entire hippocampus and a mean DSC of 0.75 across the individual subfields.

We propose a new approach to the pigeonhole phenomenon, which is a fundamental concept in quantum information theory. This method involves utilizing the transversal modes of a two-dimensional paraboloid to encode quantum states. We demonstrate that this encoding scheme is unitary and can be implemented efficiently. Furthermore, we show that the resulting states are nearly uniformly distributed across the entire Hilbert space.

This study presents a Monte Carlo simulation designed to model the capture of cosmic ray protons by the Earth's atmosphere, specifically within the Low Earth Orbit (LEO) region. The model incorporates the energy loss of protons as they traverse the atmosphere, accounting for the varying density of air at different altitudes. It also simulates the production of secondary particles resulting from proton interactions with atmospheric nuclei. The model's validity is confirmed by comparing its output with experimental data from the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS-02) on the International Space Station, which has recorded the flux of captured protons in LEO. The results indicate that the model accurately reproduces the observed energy spectrum of captured protons, with a maximum deviation of less than 10%. The study further analyzes the impact of different atmospheric models on the simulation results, demonstrating that the choice of atmospheric model has a negligible effect on the predicted flux of captured protons. The study concludes that the proposed Monte Carlo model provides a reliable and accurate method for modeling the capture of cosmic ray protons by the Earth's atmosphere in the LEO region.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a dominant approach for addressing graph-structured data challenges. However, their performance is often hindered by the inability to effectively capture both global and local graph structures. To address this, we introduce a novel framework that integrates a universal pyramid-like shrinkage skeleton with local structure link rewiring. This design enables the model to simultaneously extract global and local features, thereby enhancing the accuracy of graph-based tasks. Experimental results across multiple datasets confirm that our proposed framework achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

We introduce Huber, a framework designed to address differentially private low-rank matrix completion. Huber is a generalization of the widely used Laplace mechanism, which is currently the standard for differentially private matrix completion. We demonstrate that Huber offers a more flexible approach to achieving differential privacy. Furthermore, we show that Huber can be implemented using a variety of noise distributions, including Laplace, Gaussian, and Poisson.

The interstellar medium (ISM) is a complex mixture of gas and dust, where dust grains are responsible for the attenuation, emission, and polarization of starlight. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the physical and chemical properties of interstellar dust, specifically focusing on the diffuse ISM. It examines how dust affects starlight through attenuation, emission, and polarization, while also addressing the grain characteristics that drive these phenomena. We report the discovery of a massive planet orbiting the extremely low-mass star CIDA 1, a finding derived from a 10-year radial velocity dataset. The resulting orbit is highly eccentric ($e = 0.61 \pm 0.03$) with a period of 1,000 days, yielding a minimum planet mass of $1.6 \pm 0.1$ Jupiter masses. This companion is the most massive known to orbit a star with a mass below 0.08 solar masses. Furthermore, we present new high-resolution spectroscopic observations of CIDA 1, which reveal a significant excess of molecular absorption features in the disk's outer regions. These features are consistent with a disk sculpted by the planet's gravitational influence, a phenomenon previously observed in the HD 142527 system.

This paper introduces a new problem called "Maximum Clicks," which involves determining the minimum number of button presses required to turn all lights off on a grid. We present a polynomial-time algorithm for solving this problem on any rectangular grid. Additionally, we provide a polynomial-time algorithm for the "Lights Out" problem on a grid with holes, a known NP-complete variant. We also discuss the computational complexity of the "Maximum Clicks" problem for grids with holes.

This study introduces a novel image segmentation framework that integrates image recovery techniques to enhance partitioning outcomes. The proposed model minimizes a specific energy function, which is composed of two primary components: an image recovery term and a partitioning term. The recovery component utilizes advanced techniques, such as total variation (TV) or non-local means (NLM), to restore the image, while the partitioning component employs a Mumford-Shah type functional to segment it. The resulting partitioning model is solved using a level set method. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach yields superior segmentation quality compared to existing methods.

Abstract interpretation is a static analysis technique that approximates the semantics of a program to ensure the soundness of its results. This paper introduces a novel approach to abstract interpretation that separates the ascending and descending phases of the analysis. By leveraging this decoupling, we can apply distinct strategies to each phase, thereby enhancing the precision of the analysis.

The perovskite structure, defined by the general formula $ABO_3$, is a versatile class of materials that includes oxides, halides, and chalcogenides. These compounds are renowned for their rich and diverse physical properties, which are largely dictated by the specific arrangement of their constituent atoms. This study focuses on the phonon dispersion of the ideal $BaTiO_3$ perovskite, a material exhibiting a complex phase diagram with multiple structural phases. We demonstrate that the phonon dispersion curves are highly sensitive to the precise atomic positions within the unit cell. Furthermore, we show that the phonon spectrum can be effectively tuned by adjusting the lattice constants, a process that can be achieved through the application of external pressure or hydrostatic stress.

Detecting anomalies in high-dimensional data is a critical challenge across numerous fields, including computer vision, natural language processing, and bioinformatics. This paper introduces a novel anomaly identification approach grounded in the Closeness Graph (CG), which leverages the concept of closeness centrality to pinpoint anomalous nodes. The proposed method is highly efficient, requiring only $O(n)$ time and space complexity, and is applicable to both Euclidean and non-Euclidean metric spaces. Furthermore, it is robust against noise and outliers, making it particularly suitable for real-world applications. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that the method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study examines the interaction between a two-level atom and a perfectly conducting, slender mirror, focusing on the atom's motion within a plane perpendicular to the mirror's axis. We analyze the resulting changes in the atom's energy levels and spontaneous emission rates, which are altered by the mirror's presence. Our findings indicate that the mirror induces a significant shift in the atom's energy levels, a phenomenon that intensifies as the atom approaches the mirror. Additionally, we observe that the mirror's influence on the atom's emission rate is negligible when the atom is far away but becomes substantial at close range. We also investigate the conditions under which the mirror can either enhance or suppress the atom's emission rate. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the development of atom-mirror systems for quantum information processing.

Graphs serve as a powerful tool for modeling complex systems, yet their inherent complexity often hinders human comprehension. To address this, we introduce a new approach to graph understanding that leverages localized community equity. This method identifies communities within a graph and evaluates their equity by comparing the distribution of node attributes against a uniform distribution. We demonstrate that this metric effectively captures the essence of a community, allowing for the creation of a localized equity map that reveals the graph's underlying structure. Furthermore, we show that this map can be utilized to generate concise textual descriptions of the graph.

This study introduces a novel iterative method for solving kinetic equations governing reversible enzyme reactions, specifically those involving a single substrate and product. The approach yields estimative solutions for the time-dependent concentrations of both enzyme-substrate and enzyme-product complexes. The method's accuracy is validated by comparing its results against analytical solutions for irreversible reactions and numerical solutions for reversible reactions.

This study examines proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, focusing on final states characterized by jets and missing transverse momentum. Utilizing data collected by the ATLAS detector at the LHC, the analysis covers an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ recorded during 2015 and 32.0 fb$^{-1}$ during 2016. The investigation targets the production of a heavy neutralino, which subsequently decays into a photon and a lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP). The study also explores scenarios where the heavy neutralino is produced in pairs, with one neutralino decaying into a photon and an LSP, while the other decays into a Z boson and an LSP. The Z boson is observed to decay into either a pair of charged leptons or a pair of jets. The analysis concludes that the observed data aligns with the Standard Model predictions, with no significant deviations found. Consequently, the study establishes new exclusion limits for the heavy neutralino mass, specifically in the context of natural and split supersymmetry models.

This study introduces a new class of financial derivatives, termed "logical expectation financial swells" (LEFS), which are contingent claims whose payoff is determined by the anticipated duration of a specific event. The payoff function is defined as the product of a stochastic, mean-reverting process and a deterministic, time-dependent factor. The model is calibrated using historical data from the event's duration, the event's start time, and the event's end time. The paper presents a closed-form solution for the pricing of LEFS and provides a numerical analysis of the model's sensitivity to various parameters.

This study examines a quantum harmonic oscillator subjected to a constant external force, with its dynamics analyzed through the Feynman path integral formalism. We employ the Metropolis algorithm within a Markov chain Monte Carlo framework to numerically evaluate the path integral, specifically calculating the propagator and the ground state wave function. Furthermore, we derive the ground state energy and the expectation value of the position operator.

Item recommendation systems are essential for e-commerce platforms, yet they frequently fail to capture the nuanced sentiment expressed in user reviews. This study introduces a new approach that integrates sentiment analysis into the recommendation process by leveraging evaluation data. Specifically, we propose a Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) designed to jointly model sentiment and recommendation tasks. The SIFN architecture employs a multi-layer fusion mechanism to capture sentiment-aware interactions between user and item representations. Furthermore, it utilizes a sentiment-sensitive gating network to dynamically regulate the flow of sentiment information during the recommendation process. Experimental results demonstrate that the SIFN model significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study investigates the use of lexical substitutions to enhance Arabic-English code-switched information. We introduce a novel approach to augmenting Arabic-English code-switched datasets by applying word-level substitutions, which are then evaluated through a comparative analysis of various substitution techniques. The findings indicate that our proposed method significantly outperforms existing approaches, resulting in a substantial increase in the quality of Arabic-English code-switched information.
We demonstrate that the collection of homeomorphisms of a closed surface with a bounded displacement metric is Roelcke precompact if and only if it is finite.

We introduce a generalized $\lambda$-transformation applicable to a broad class of Lagrangian densities, which encompasses the standard $\lambda$-transformation as a specific instance. This transformation yields a new Lagrangian that generates equations of motion equivalent to those of the original system. We demonstrate that the original and transformed Lagrangians are linked by a canonical transformation. Furthermore, we establish that the transformation maps the original Hamiltonian to a new Hamiltonian that is canonically conjugate to it. Finally, we illustrate the utility of this approach by applying it to the Lagrangian describing a membrane in an AdS$_4$ black hole background.

We introduce a new algorithm for generating a valid vertex ordering in hex meshes, a task that is NP-hard. Our approach relies on a novel graph-theoretic result: every hex mesh can be decomposed into a sequence of tetrahedra, where each tetrahedron shares exactly one face with the preceding one. This decomposition is achieved by finding a Hamiltonian path in a specific auxiliary graph. We prove that this auxiliary graph is always Hamiltonian, and we provide a polynomial-time algorithm to construct the path. Our method is highly efficient, capable of processing meshes with millions of vertices in mere milliseconds.

Relation extraction aims to identify the semantic connections between entities within a sentence. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages knowledge graph connection prediction to enhance relation extraction. Specifically, we utilize a knowledge graph to identify potential semantic relations between entities and then employ a relation classifier to determine the precise relation type. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art relation extraction models.

This paper introduces a method for analytically calculating the delay of a full-wave rectifier, which is a critical parameter in power supply design. The study utilizes a full-wave rectifier circuit as a case study, employing a piecewise linear model for the diode to derive an analytical expression for the delay. The resulting formula is validated through a MATLAB simulation that compares the calculated delay against the actual delay observed in a real diode.

This paper introduces a new concept of rough-grained smoothness, which generalizes the traditional Lipschitz continuity used in reinforcement learning. We demonstrate that this new smoothness property is equivalent to the Lipschitz continuity of a function's distribution under the Wasserstein metric. Leveraging this equivalence, we establish a novel framework for analyzing the smoothness of value functions in Markov decision processes (MDPs). We prove that the optimal value function in a continuous-state MDP is rough-grained smooth with respect to the Wasserstein metric, and we derive rough-grained smoothness bounds for the Q-function under the same metric. Furthermore, we show that the rough-grained smoothness of the Q-function is essential for deriving the sample complexity of approximate dynamic programming (ADP) algorithms. Finally, we provide rough-grained smoothness bounds for the Q-function in both discounted and average-reward MDPs.

Although animacy is a fundamental trait of objects, its neural representation within the human ventral temporal cortex (VTC) remains unclear. This study investigates the spatial organization of animacy in the VTC using high-resolution fMRI data from 12 participants. We employed a novel approach to map animacy gradients by analyzing the similarity of neural responses to animate versus inanimate stimuli. Our findings reveal that the VTC contains a continuous animacy gradient, with animate objects eliciting stronger activation in the anterior regions and inanimate objects in the posterior regions. Furthermore, we observed that this gradient is more pronounced in the left hemisphere than in the right. These results indicate that animacy is not localized to a specific area but is instead distributed across the VTC in a graded manner.

This study introduces a new filter designed to preserve the geometric structure of finite element simulations, specifically maintaining the positive semi-definiteness of the Hessian matrix. By leveraging convex optimization, the filter ensures that the resulting smoothed function remains twice differentiable, thereby avoiding the numerical instabilities associated with non-smooth operations like absolute values. The approach is demonstrated through a two-dimensional simulation of a nonlinear elastic material, where the filtered Hessian is utilized to solve a nonlinear inverse problem.

This study investigates the corona's evolution in the black hole binary MAXI J1535-571 using Insight-HXMT data, specifically focusing on the type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) observed during the 2018 outburst. By analyzing the QPO frequency and the power ratio of the hard X-ray band (20–60 keV) to the soft X-ray band (2–10 keV), we tracked the corona's development. Our findings indicate that the type-C QPO frequency rises as the hard-to-soft X-ray power ratio increases, a trend consistent with the corona expanding outward from the black hole. Furthermore, the corona's size is estimated to be approximately 10–15 gravitational radii ($R_g$) during the hard state and roughly 2–3 $R_g$ during the soft state.

This study introduces a novel framework for social robotics, termed "Social Inherent Motivation" (SIM), designed to enable robots to autonomously learn and execute socially appropriate behaviors. The core concept posits that a robot is driven to acquire skills that facilitate its interaction with a human partner. The proposed system integrates a transfer learning mechanism, allowing the robot to adapt previously learned skills to new scenarios. The research demonstrates that this approach allows a robot to effectively learn and execute socially relevant actions, such as mimicking a human's movements or following them, by leveraging transfer learning.

We introduce a novel, single-shot approach for identifying any material, regardless of its state, by leveraging a physics-informed contrastive learning framework. This method utilizes a physics-based simulator to generate synthetic data, which is then employed to train a neural network capable of distinguishing between different substances. The resulting model is subsequently fine-tuned on real-world experimental data. This strategy enables the identification of unknown substances from a single image, even when the substances are chemically similar.

This paper provides a survey of Lie 2-groups, which are 2-group analogues of Lie groups. We examine their fundamental properties, including their relationship to Lie 2-algebras, and offer a classification of abelian Lie 2-groups. Additionally, we outline the concept of a Lie 2-group action on a Lie 2-space and demonstrate how such actions correspond to representations of the underlying Lie 2-algebra.

This paper introduces LoFTR, a novel, detector-free framework for matching local features. Unlike traditional methods that rely on handcrafted descriptors, LoFTR utilizes a transformer-based architecture to extract and match features directly from image regions. By employing a self-attention mechanism, the model captures long-range dependencies to establish correspondences between local features. Furthermore, LoFTR incorporates a cross-attention module to facilitate the interaction between query and key features, enhancing the robustness of the matching process. Experimental results demonstrate that LoFTR achieves state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks, including the Paris, 7-Scenes, and KITTI datasets.

Solar vector magnetic field data are essential for investigating the Sun's magnetic field and its influence on space weather. These measurements are typically obtained by analyzing the polarization of spectral lines, which are subsequently processed to generate vector magnetic field information. However, this processing can introduce biases that distort the resulting data. This study examines the origins of such biases and proposes methods to mitigate them.

This study introduces a self-governing demand-side management framework that utilizes Energy Usage Planning (EUP) and immediate load invoicing. The proposed system is designed to enhance the operational efficiency of the power grid and empower consumers to actively participate in grid management. The underlying mechanism relies on an aggregative game, where consumers optimize their energy consumption by considering the collective behavior of the group. The paper details the mathematical formulation of this game, establishes its existence and uniqueness, and demonstrates that the resulting equilibrium is Pareto optimal. Furthermore, the authors present a distributed algorithm for computing the equilibrium, which is proven to converge to the unique solution. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through numerical simulations.

This study examines the influence of Rastall theory on the emission of charged black strings, specifically focusing on the Rastall parameter's impact on the Hawking temperature and the emission rate of massive particles. The analysis reveals that the Rastall parameter significantly alters the Hawking temperature, thereby affecting the emission rate of massive particles. Additionally, the study explores the influence of the Rastall parameter on the emission rate of massless particles, finding that it also plays a significant role in this process. The study concludes that the Rastall parameter has a profound impact on the emission rate of both massive and massless particles, thereby influencing the overall dynamics of charged black strings.

This paper examines the convergence rate of von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem, specifically focusing on the spectral measure of a unitary operator $U$ on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ relative to a given vector $f \in \mathcal{H}$. We establish that the speed of convergence is governed by the distance between this spectral measure and the Dirac measure $\delta_1$ located at $1$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the rate of convergence is equivalent to the Wasserstein distance between the spectral measure and $\delta_1$.

The Gaia mission is expected to identify approximately 100 million stars within the Milky Way, with a significant portion of these being metal-poor. This study introduces a novel technique for detecting metal-poor stars using Gaia's Blue-Photometer and Red-Photometer spectra. The method relies on the fact that metal-poor stars exhibit a distinct spectral feature at 4000 Å, which is absent in metal-rich stars. We demonstrate that this feature can be identified by analyzing the second derivative of the flux spectrum. Furthermore, we show that the method's effectiveness is enhanced by applying a specific wavelength range selection.

This study presents a novel method for forecasting the intensity of worldwide blazes, which are defined as large-scale fires occurring in the boreal forests of the Northern Hemisphere. These fires are driven by the seasonal thawing of permafrost, which releases trapped methane and accelerates global warming. The research utilizes a dataset of 100 years of fire records from the MODIS satellite to analyze the relationship between fire intensity and the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon. The findings indicate that the intensity of these fires is significantly correlated with ENSO, a major driver of global climate variability. Furthermore, the study introduces a new prediction model capable of estimating the intensity of worldwide blazes based on ENSO data.

We investigate the gravitational lensing characteristics of galaxy clusters and groups, specifically examining the impact of Self-Interacting Dark Matter (SIDM) on the inner regions of their dark matter halos. By utilizing the cluster lensing tool (CLT) to analyze the lensing properties of 100 clusters and groups from the SDSS DR12 catalog, we identify 10 minor-scale lenses. These systems are analyzed using the CLT to determine their mass profiles, which are then compared against predictions from the standard Cold Dark Matter (CDM) model and the SIDM model. Our findings indicate that the mass profiles of these minor-scale lenses are consistent with both CDM and SIDM scenarios. However, we observe that SIDM models predict a steeper inner density slope than CDM, a discrepancy that could potentially be resolved by incorporating baryonic effects.

We introduce a model reduction framework that leverages a model's partial insights to construct a simplified version. This approach is grounded in a novel concept of model distance, defined as the maximum discrepancy between the original and simplified models across all possible inputs. We demonstrate that this distance metric is equivalent to the Wasserstein distance between the models' output distributions. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical bound linking the approximation error to this distance. Finally, we present a practical algorithm for computing the model distance and illustrate its application in reducing a complex, high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical system.

This paper introduces a new algorithm named M-ar-K-Fast (M-ar-K-Fast), designed to perform unsupervised feature extraction for high-dimensional data. The method is grounded in the concept of a "local manifold," which is defined as a low-dimensional structure embedded within a high-dimensional space. The proposed approach utilizes a weighted local manifold to capture the intrinsic geometric characteristics of the data. The algorithm's performance is evaluated using two distinct datasets: the MNIST handwritten digit set and the Caltech-101 object recognition set. The results demonstrate that M-ar-K-Fast achieves superior performance compared to several existing state-of-the-art algorithms.

Social media platforms serve as a primary source for real-time information, yet the vast volume of user-generated content makes it difficult to extract meaningful insights. This study introduces a novel framework for identifying spatial-temporal events from geotagged social media posts. The approach begins by automatically detecting event boundaries through a clustering algorithm, followed by the application of a novel event identification method that leverages both textual and spatial data. This method employs a sliding window technique to analyze the temporal evolution of event characteristics, enabling the real-time identification of emerging events. The system was evaluated using a dataset of 1.5 million geotagged tweets from the 2012 US Presidential Election, demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying event boundaries and tracking their development.
This paper investigates the existence of solutions to a specific class of elliptic equations, which arise in the context of prescribing metrics on surfaces.

This study presents a computational investigation into yttrium-cobalt-boron alloys, a system of significant interest for developing high-performance permanent magnets. By employing evolutionary algorithms, we identified numerous stable compounds, including several with high cobalt content. Our analysis of the electronic and magnetic properties of these materials reveals that the majority exhibit ferromagnetism, with the exception of a few that display antiferromagnetic behavior. Furthermore, we identified a specific compound, YCo$_{11}$B$_{2}$, which possesses a high Curie temperature and a substantial magnetic moment.

This study addresses the challenge of bidding for display advertising within a budget-constrained environment. We introduce a novel adaptive bidding strategy that dynamically adjusts bid prices based on real-time data regarding impression quality and conversion rates. This approach is designed to maximize the number of conversions while strictly adhering to a predefined budget. We rigorously analyze the algorithm's performance, establishing theoretical upper bounds for both the expected conversion count and the risk of budget exhaustion. Furthermore, we validate the method's effectiveness through extensive experiments using real-world data from a leading Chinese display advertising platform.

We investigate the quantum guidance principle, which posits that a quantum system's evolution is directed by its wave function. This principle is examined through the lens of the Wigner function, a quasi-probability distribution defined over phase space. We demonstrate that whenever the Wigner function remains non-negative, the quantum guidance principle fails to hold.

This study introduces a novel privacy amplification method for quantum key exchange (QKD) that eliminates the need for uniform random sources. By employing a non-uniform random source, the approach achieves a tighter bound on the QKD security parameter compared to standard techniques. The authors present a specific privacy amplification protocol utilizing a non-uniform random source and derive a corresponding bound on the QKD security parameter. The analysis demonstrates that this new bound is strictly tighter than the conventional bound derived under the assumption of a uniform random source. Furthermore, the study provides a concrete example illustrating the practical application of this improved security bound.

This paper examines the geometry of timelike curves in semi-Riemannian space, specifically focusing on those that are both Bertrand and satisfy the condition where the principal normal vector field is parallel. We establish the necessary and sufficient criteria for a curve to be classified as a timelike Bertrand curve within this framework. Furthermore, we derive the specific conditions required for such curves to be helices.

This paper examines the distribution of the sum of two independent Feller diffusion processes, which are defined as non-negative, continuous-time Markov chains. We demonstrate that the resulting distribution can be expressed as a weighted sum of Feller diffusion distributions, where the weights are determined by a specific combinatorial distribution. Furthermore, we derive the probability generating function for this combinatorial distribution and establish its convergence to a Poisson distribution under a specific limiting condition.

We introduce a diagrammatic approach to analyze the scattering of multi-photon configurations within waveguide quantum electrodynamics (QED). This method is applicable to systems featuring a single two-level emitter coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide. By employing a Dyson equation, we derive the scattering matrix for an arbitrary number of photons, expressed as a sum over all possible scattering diagrams. Each diagram corresponds to a specific term in the scattering matrix, with its amplitude determined by the emitter's Green's function and the associated scattering processes. We demonstrate the method's utility by calculating the scattering matrix for two-photon configurations, revealing that the resulting amplitudes are governed by the emitter's Green's function and the specific scattering pathways. Furthermore, we show that the method can be extended to systems with multiple emitters, where the scattering matrix is given by a sum over all possible scattering diagrams involving the emitters' Green's functions and scattering processes. Finally, we discuss the implications of the method for understanding the scattering of multi-photon configurations in waveguide QED systems.

We investigate the impact of spin-dependent interactions on the dark matter (DM) density profile within the Milky Way's central region. Our findings indicate that, for a fixed total DM mass, the central density is significantly higher when spin-dependent interactions are present compared to scenarios where only spin-independent interactions occur. This enhancement arises because spin-dependent interactions are more effective at transferring angular momentum to DM particles, thereby facilitating their outward diffusion. Consequently, the central density can be amplified by a factor of approximately 100. This result holds particular relevance for the indirect detection of DM, as the annihilation rate is highly sensitive to the density in the galactic core.

This paper examines the Faulhaber formula for summing odd powers of integers, a formula originally derived by Johann Faulhaber in 1545. It also explores the connection between Faulhaber's coefficients and the Euler zigzag numbers, which Faulhaber referred to as "tangent numbers."

This study introduces a novel non-coherent differential detection method for continuous phase modulation (CPM) signals, designed to enhance the delay of traditional non-coherent differential detectors. The proposed approach achieves a delay improvement of $2T_b$ over conventional methods, where $T_b$ represents the bit duration. Theoretical analysis and simulation results confirm that this new technique maintains the same bit error rate (BER) performance as the traditional non-coherent differential detector.

Reward learning is a critical component of reinforcement learning, yet it remains a difficult task for humans. This paper introduces a novel approach to reward learning that leverages human visual capabilities. The method involves presenting users with a set of state-action pairs and asking them to rank these pairs based on their desirability. By utilizing a clustering algorithm, the system organizes these pairs into groups, allowing the user to rank the clusters rather than every individual pair. This strategy significantly reduces the cognitive load on the user. Furthermore, the system employs a neural network to infer the reward function from these human rankings. Experimental results indicate that this approach is both effective and efficient.

We investigate the impact of noncommutative spacetime on nucleon structure functions, specifically examining the nucleon's partonic makeup. By employing the nucleon's light-front wave function, we derive the corresponding parton distribution functions (PDFs) and find that the nucleon's composition remains largely unaffected by noncommutative effects.

We introduce a new class of frustrated pattern models, defined by a lattice of plaquettes where each is assigned a pattern of four distinct colors. These models serve as a generalization of the Toric code, which corresponds to a system with only two colors. We demonstrate that the ground state of the Hamiltonian is characterized by a topological order, featuring a non-trivial ground state degeneracy that depends on the system's genus. Furthermore, we show that the system supports topological edge states, which can be described by a chiral topological field theory.

This paper investigates the complex alteration of random band matrices, a model that interpolates between random matrices and random matrices. We demonstrate that the complex alteration of random matrices exhibits a phase transition, which is characterized by a sigma-model.

This study introduces a new pre-training approach for dialogue comprehension, leveraging the semantic relationships between utterances. We propose a new pre-training task that utilizes a meaning representation to capture the semantic essence of conversations. By employing a meaning-aware model, we demonstrate that this method significantly enhances performance on dialogue comprehension tasks.

Interpretability is a critical factor in the deployment of machine learning algorithms, particularly in high-stakes domains like healthcare and finance. While existing research predominantly focuses on post-hoc methods that explain model predictions, this study introduces a new framework for assessing algorithmic interpretability from a human-learning perspective. We propose that an algorithm is interpretable if a human can learn to replicate its decision-making process. To operationalize this, we developed a Cognitive Complexity Score (CCS) that quantifies the difficulty of learning an algorithm by measuring the cognitive load required to emulate it. We evaluated the CCS across 100 algorithms from the OpenML benchmark, covering 10 distinct families and 10 datasets. Our findings reveal a strong positive correlation between CCS and human prediction accuracy, indicating that algorithms with lower cognitive complexity are easier for humans to learn. Furthermore, we observed that CCS correlates positively with model complexity and negatively with human performance. These results underscore the necessity of considering human learning capabilities when designing interpretable algorithms.

The Isolation Forest (iForest) algorithm is a popular unsupervised outlier detection method that identifies anomalies by isolating data points within a tree structure. This study introduces TiWS-iForest, a novel variant designed to enhance performance in scenarios with limited data and minimal supervision. The proposed approach incorporates two key mechanisms: a weighted sampling strategy that prioritizes minority classes, and a weighted isolation criterion that adjusts the significance of outliers based on their class distribution. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that TiWS-iForest outperforms existing outlier detection methods, particularly in small-scale, weakly supervised environments.

This paper introduces a reparametrization of the Poisson process that facilitates the estimation of extreme values. By leveraging this new framework, we develop a Bayesian estimator for the tail of a distribution, which is subsequently validated through a simulation study.

This study examines the mean cross-sectional area of a closed curve within a specific region of the plane. We demonstrate that the set of such regions where this mean value remains constant is not necessarily a single connected component. Furthermore, we establish the existence of closed curves with a fixed mean cross-sectional area that possess a non-zero mean curvature.

This paper introduces the COMET-ATOMIC 2020 shared task, which focuses on leveraging common sense knowledge for natural language inference. The Atomic dataset, a comprehensive repository of common sense knowledge, serves as the foundation for this study. The task is divided into two tracks: Track A involves training a neural network to predict the entailment relationship between premise and hypothesis pairs, while Track B requires generating symbolic logical rules to represent these relationships. The paper details the dataset, outlines the specific objectives of both tracks, and presents the results achieved by participating teams.

We present a high-precision study of the chemical composition in NGC 2808, a globular cluster known for its complex horizontal branch (HB) morphology. By analyzing 100 high-resolution spectra of HB stars, we determined their abundances of 11 elements (C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Ti, Cr, Fe) and derived the mean metallicity as [Fe/H] = -0.61 ± 0.03. Our findings reveal a significant spread in [α/Fe] ratios, ranging from 0.1 to 0.4 dex, which aligns with previous studies of HB stars in this cluster. Additionally, we identified a correlation between [α/Fe] and [Fe/H] that mirrors the "alpha-dip" observed in the main sequence of NGC 2808. These results confirm that the HB morphology in NGC 2808 arises from a mix of stars with varying chemical compositions, a conclusion supported by the detection of a distinct [α/Fe] gradient across the HB.

This study examines the initial exit duration statistics of Sole File Distribution (SFD) users, a method for distributing large files via peer-to-peer networks. We analyze the distribution of the time required for a user to download a file from a single source, a metric that is critical for evaluating SFD performance. Our findings indicate that this initial exit duration follows a power-law distribution, a result that aligns with the power-law characteristics observed in the complete download duration. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of entropic power to characterize the initial exit duration distribution. We demonstrate that the entropic power of the initial exit duration is significantly lower than that of the total download duration, a difference that increases as the number of peers in the SFD system grows.
