This paper introduces a shape expression framework designed to validate relational schemas and facilitate the conversion of relational data into RDF. It defines a set of shape expressions that can be applied to relational schemas to ensure their validity. Furthermore, it outlines a method for transforming relational data into RDF while adhering to these shape constraints.

The pyStoNED library is a Python-based tool designed to estimate the Stochastic Nonparametric Efficiency Decomposition (StoNED) model, originally proposed by Kneip and Stoker (1996). StoNED is a nonparametric regression framework that decomposes the error term into two components: one representing heterogeneity across entities and another capturing temporal variation. This approach is particularly valuable for analyzing panel data where the number of entities is large but the time dimension is small. The library's primary objective is to compute the efficiency scores of decision-making units (DMUs) by regressing their outputs on inputs, thereby isolating the stochastic noise from the underlying production technology. The resulting efficiency scores are subsequently used to evaluate the performance of these units.

This study examines the $t \bar t \phi$ production channel at the LHC, where $\phi$ represents a heavy scalar particle. We analyze the process as a potential mechanism for generating the observed dark matter abundance, specifically focusing on the scenario where $\phi$ is a dark matter candidate. Furthermore, we investigate the possibility of $\phi$ being a heavy Higgs boson, which could arise from an extended Higgs sector. Our analysis includes a detailed examination of the $t \bar t \phi$ cross-section, the associated production rates, and the resulting experimental signatures.

We introduce a novel approach to analyzing pretrained language models (PLMs) that requires neither human supervision nor extensive labeled data. By leveraging the PLM's own internal representations, our method identifies and isolates the specific features responsible for a model's predictions. This technique enables the creation of targeted interventions to correct errors and offers a deeper understanding of the model's decision-making process. We demonstrate the utility of this approach through two applications: (1) correcting classification errors in the GLUE benchmark, and (2) generating explanations for predictions made on the CoLA dataset.

This paper introduces an open-source speech identification system for German, developed using the DeepSpeech 2 framework. The system was trained on the German Common Voice dataset, which contains 10,000 hours of speech data. The authors evaluated the model's performance on the German subset of the Common Voice benchmark, achieving a word error rate of 10.1%.

We present a study of 12 Be-type stars in the 30 Doradus region, utilizing high-resolution spectra from the VLT/UVES instrument. Our analysis reveals that these stars exhibit a wide range of rotational velocities, with projected rotational velocities ($v \sin i$) spanning from 100 to 300 km/s. Additionally, we observed significant variability in the He II $\lambda$4686 emission line, which is attributed to the stars' rapid rotation. Our findings indicate that the majority of these objects are likely Be stars in a post-main-sequence evolutionary stage.

Inverse Text Standardization (ITS) is a critical component in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that converts informal text, such as chat messages, into standard language. This study investigates the efficacy of data augmentation techniques in improving ITS models. We demonstrate that applying augmentation strategies to the training set significantly boosts model performance. Furthermore, we introduce a novel augmentation method that leverages the contextual information of the input to generate synthetic samples, which also yields substantial improvements.
This paper establishes a Faber-Krahn inequality for the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator, subject to Robin boundary conditions on the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

We introduce a new class of cores, termed NFT cores, which are non-exchangeable and non-trivial. These cores are defined by a specific set of properties that are shown to be both necessary and sufficient for the existence of an NFT core. We also provide an example of an NFT core that is not a tangent core, thereby demonstrating that the class of tangent cores is a proper subset of the class of NFT cores.

We investigate the topological characteristics of a non-Hermitian one-dimensional lattice featuring a point gap, where particle interactions are introduced. Our findings indicate that these interactions can diminish the non-trivial point-gap topology, a phenomenon that is not captured by the conventional winding number. To address this, we introduce a new topological invariant, the winding number of the eigenstates, which remains robust against interaction effects. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the emergence of a winding number gap is accompanied by the appearance of a winding number gapless point, a signature that can be detected through the winding number of the eigenstates.

This study investigates the synthesis of speech imbued with specific social characteristics, such as gender and age. We introduce a novel framework that synthesizes speech with these social traits by leveraging a speaker embedding model trained on the VoxCeleb2 dataset. This approach enables the generation of speech with defined social attributes from any source speaker. Furthermore, we present a new dataset, VoxCeleb2-Social, which includes social trait labels for VoxCeleb2 speakers. Experimental results demonstrate that our method successfully synthesizes speech with specified social traits while maintaining the original speaker's identity.

We propose a model featuring a gauged $U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry alongside a discrete $A_4$ symmetry, which serves as a source of modular symmetry. This framework allows for the spontaneous breaking of $U(1)_{B-L}$ at a high energy scale, thereby generating a right-handed Majorana neutrino mass and a $Z$ boson. The model is constructed to be free of anomalies and remains consistent with experimental constraints. Furthermore, it offers a viable mechanism for dark matter stability and explains the observed baryon asymmetry of the universe through leptogenesis.

This study examines the collective dynamics of triaxial nuclei using the minimal distance concept, a framework that defines the collective coordinates as the shortest distance between the nuclear surface and a triaxial ellipsoid. We demonstrate that the collective Hamiltonian derived from this approach is consistent with the Bohr-Mottelson Hamiltonian, which is expressed in terms of the triaxial ellipsoid's deformation parameters. Furthermore, we analyze the collective motion of the triaxial nucleus $^{152}$Gd, which exhibits a well-defined triaxial deformation.

This paper presents a design methodology for constructing polyphase Golay complementary structures (PCSs) with arbitrary lengths, utilizing the properties of Golay complementary sequences (PCSs) and Golay complementary pairs (PCPs) of real-valued length $N$. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any prime $p$ and any integer $N$ where $\gcd(N, p) = 1$, there exist $p$ polyphase Golay complementary structures (PCSs) of length $N$. Furthermore, we establish the existence of $p^2$ polyphase Golay complementary structures (PCSs) of length $N$ when $p$ is a prime and $\gcd(N, p) = 1$.

This study introduces a novel unsupervised approach for detecting alterations in hyperspectral imagery (HSI) by leveraging deep convolutional autoencoders (CAEs). The method begins by training a deep CNN on a large dataset of natural images to extract high-level features, which are then integrated with the outputs of a shallow CNN trained specifically on the HSI data. This combined feature set is subsequently fed into a deep convolutional autoencoder to learn a compact representation of the images. Finally, an alteration map is generated by comparing the reconstruction errors of the original and altered images. The efficacy of this proposed framework is validated through experiments on two benchmark datasets: the Washington DC Mall and the Pavia University.

This study examines the link between residual entropy and viscosity in molecular fluids, utilizing both simulation data and theoretical frameworks. We analyze the temperature-dependent viscosity of Lennard-Jones (LJ) fluids and hard-sphere (HS) fluids through molecular dynamics simulations, alongside the viscosity of a Lennard-Jones fluid with a dipole moment using Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we calculate the residual entropy of these systems using the two-body approximation. Our findings indicate that the temperature dependence of viscosity in both HS and LJ fluids aligns with the residual entropy's temperature behavior. We further explore the relationship between viscosity and residual entropy using the Adam-Gibbs equation, which demonstrates a strong correlation between the two variables.

This study examines a cyclical cosmological model featuring a $\Lambda$-driven accelerated expansion phase followed by a Big Rip singularity, which is succeeded by a new Big Bang. We demonstrate that the $\Lambda$ parameter can be interpreted as a dark energy density that undergoes a sign reversal during the transition from the Big Rip to the subsequent Big Bang. Furthermore, we analyze the evolution of the scale factor and the Hubble parameter across the entire cyclical timeline.

This study explores the possibility of concealing variables within a superdeterministic framework, specifically utilizing the Invariant-set theory proposed by Gribbin. We demonstrate that the Invariant-set concept can be integrated into a concealed-variable model, thereby accounting for the correlations observed in Bell-type experiments.

Keyphrase detection involves identifying the most relevant terms within a document that best encapsulate its core meaning. This study introduces a neural network architecture designed to detect keyphrases in IoT gadgets, a domain where such tasks are typically hindered by scarce labeled data. The proposed method employs a multi-task learning framework that simultaneously trains on two distinct datasets: one for keyphrase detection and another for keyphrase generation. By leveraging the generative task to create synthetic training data, the model effectively mitigates the limitations of limited labeled inputs. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms baseline models, achieving a 10% increase in F1-score.

This study examines the statistical mechanics of two-dimensional fermions interacting with a background gauge field, a framework that yields a dimer model featuring a complex weight. We demonstrate that the critical behavior of this model is governed by a Dirac fermion theory, which is coupled to the background field. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between the dimer model's partition function and the fermionic theory's partition function, a relationship that holds true even in the presence of the background gauge field.

Group Lasso is a popular technique for variable selection in high-dimensional settings, where variables are organized into groups based on shared characteristics. While this approach is effective for continuous data, it is less suitable for categorical variables because standard methods rely on Euclidean distances, which are not well-defined for such data. To address this, we introduce a novel Group Lasso framework that incorporates categorical information by utilizing a specific distance metric. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness through simulations and a real-world application involving the analysis of gene expression data across various cancer types.

This paper introduces T-Visor, a hypervisor designed for mixed-criticality embedded real-time systems that leverages hardware virtualization to support both high-importance and low-importance tasks. By utilizing the Intel VT-x architecture, T-Visor enables the virtualization of the physical processor, memory, and I/O subsystems. The hypervisor manages the scheduling of virtual machines (VMs) and virtual devices, while also handling the allocation of physical resources to these VMs. To ensure strict adherence to real-time constraints, T-Visor employs a preemptive scheduling strategy for VMs and implements a non-preemptive approach for virtual devices. Furthermore, the system incorporates a mechanism to detect and mitigate the impact of virtualization-induced overhead on real-time performance.

This study introduces a novel panoramic stitching technique that leverages gravity preference to enhance image alignment. By utilizing the gravity vector, the method identifies the most suitable image regions for stitching, thereby reducing computational costs and improving accuracy. Additionally, the approach employs a minimalistic strategy to optimize the camera's intrinsic parameters, ensuring robust performance even with limited data.

This study examines a system of two coupled populations, each containing $N$ neurons, where the neurons within a single group are identical and subject to the same noise. The groups are linked by a common excitatory connection. The analysis focuses on the system's variability, which is quantified by the ratio of the standard deviation of the population's mean activity to the standard deviation of individual neuron activity. The findings indicate that this variability ratio remains constant regardless of the number of neurons per group. Furthermore, the system exhibits a chimera state characterized by one population displaying synchronous activity while the other remains asynchronous. The transition between these states is governed by the coupling strength, which can be determined analytically.

This paper introduces a model-driven approach for stochastic policy optimization aimed at generating resilient controllers for nonlinear systems. The proposed method utilizes a model-based policy gradient algorithm to efficiently explore the policy space, thereby enhancing the likelihood of discovering resilient solutions. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the policy gradient estimator remains unbiased and exhibits a bounded variance. Furthermore, the study establishes a convergence rate for the policy gradient algorithm, which is contingent upon the accuracy of the system model. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through numerical experiments on a nonlinear inverted pendulum system.

We introduce a new class of graphs, termed multi-layer graphs, which are defined by a set of directed edges and a set of directed loops. These structures are designed to facilitate the construction of associative algebras that are elevated slice algebras.

We introduce a stochastic tensor network framework designed to model the dynamics of quantum systems. This approach enables the computation of the entropy of a quantum state, which is represented as a stochastic tensor network. We demonstrate that this entropy can be expressed as a sum of two components: a "direct" entropy and a "mirrored" entropy. The direct entropy is calculated using a straightforward contraction of the network, whereas the mirrored entropy arises from a more complex structure. We establish a connection between this mirrored entropy and the complexity of the underlying stochastic tensor network. Furthermore, we show that the mirrored entropy can be approximated by a variational principle, which facilitates its numerical estimation.

We investigate the stochastic dynamics of a population of $N$ individuals, where each person possesses a heritable binary trait. This trait is transmitted to offspring with a probability of $1-\epsilon$, where $\epsilon$ represents the mutation rate. The population size remains constant, and individuals reproduce according to a birth-death process. We analyze the system's behavior across three distinct regimes: (i) $\epsilon \ll 1/N$, (ii) $\epsilon \gg 1/N$, and (iii) $\epsilon \approx 1/N$. In the first regime, the population consists of a single lineage that persists for an exponentially long duration, allowing the system to be modeled as a Markov chain. The second regime is characterized by rapid lineage turnover, resulting in a Markovian process that is effectively memoryless. The third regime exhibits complex dynamics, where the system's evolution depends on the history of the population. This study examines the three-dimensional generalized Hénon map, a system defined by three parameters. We analyze the system's dynamics, specifically focusing on the bifurcation diagram and the resulting attractors.

This study examines the gravitational curvature of a solitary particle, a concept that extends the framework of the gravitational field of a single particle. We demonstrate that the curvature tensor for a lone particle is not a solitary entity but rather a collection of tensors, each corresponding to a specific rank. Furthermore, we establish that the gravitational curvature of a solitary particle is not a static property but evolves over time.

This paper examines the distribution of hook lengths in Young diagrams that are divisible by two or three. We establish that the logarithm of the count of standard Young tableaux with hook lengths divisible by two or three follows a normal distribution, and we determine the corresponding mean and variance.

We introduce a novel approach to measuring the tunneling duration of a particle, utilizing the Larmor clock method. This technique involves passing the particle through a weak magnetic field, which induces a spin precession; the resulting shift in the final spin state serves as a proxy for the tunneling time. Our findings indicate that this duration is governed by the spin oscillation period within the tunneling region. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the tunneling time can be modulated by adjusting the particle's spin orientation.

This study examines the dominant twist distribution functions for P-wave nonrelativistic mesons, which are defined as the leading contributions to the hadronic matrix elements of the corresponding operators. We derive the analytical forms of these distribution functions for both $^{3}P_{0}$ and $^{3}P_{1}$ mesons, demonstrating that they are expressed as polynomials in the momentum fraction variable $\xi$. Furthermore, we calculate the corresponding moments and analyze the behavior of these distribution functions under various limits.

We introduce a nonlinear quantum operator that models the dynamics of a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) within a Bose-Hubbard framework. This operator is defined as a power series in the bosonic creation and annihilation operators, with coefficients determined by the BEC's ground state wave function. By employing this operator, we derive the BEC's time evolution and establish a corresponding nonlinear quantum Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the expectation values of the bosonic operators in the BEC's ground state align with the classical equations of motion governing the system.

We demonstrate that the double soft theorem for gravitons is equivalent to the Ward identity associated with asymptotic symmetries in the context of celestial holography. Furthermore, we establish that the double soft theorem for photons corresponds to the Ward identity for asymptotic symmetries within the celestial sphere.

Continual learning addresses the challenge of acquiring new knowledge sequentially without forgetting previously learned tasks. While existing research predominantly focuses on individual learners, this study investigates a collective setting where multiple agents acquire knowledge from a shared data stream. We introduce a novel framework for online collective continual learning, enabling agents to learn collaboratively while retaining access to their own historical data. To achieve this, we propose a neural architecture that facilitates the sharing of knowledge among agents. Furthermore, we develop a learning algorithm that allows agents to update their models using both their private data and the aggregated information from the group. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in online collective continual learning.

This work introduces a generalized concept of a shape applicable to any subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$, extending the notion of a measure to $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a four-dimensional object. We demonstrate that the space of Ricci flat four-measures is convex and establish the existence of Ricci flat four-measures with prescribed support. Furthermore, we prove that any four-measure can be approximated by a sequence of Ricci flat four-measures.

This paper investigates permutation functions from $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$ to itself, where $q$ is a prime power. We establish that any such function can be expressed as a composition of a linear transformation and a function of the form $f(x^q+x)$, where $f$ is a permutation on $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$. Additionally, we provide a complete classification of these functions that induce the identity map on the subfield $\mathbb{F}_q$.

This study presents a deep belief network (DBN) approach for classifying intestinal worms, a task critical for diagnosing parasitic infections. The proposed method leverages the DBN's ability to learn complex, non-linear feature representations from raw data, thereby enhancing classification accuracy. Experimental results indicate that the DBN outperforms traditional classifiers, achieving a 99.1% accuracy rate.

This study examines a class of non-zero-sum investment and reinsurance games involving two competing insurers. The surplus dynamics of each insurer are modeled as a regime-switching jump-diffusion process, where the regime represents the current economic environment. The first insurer seeks to maximize the expected discounted utility of terminal wealth, while the second aims to maximize the expected discounted utility of terminal surplus. The analysis focuses on deriving the optimal investment and reinsurance strategies for both parties.

This study introduces a novel, two-stage approach for solving the fluid dynamics equations governing flight. The first stage employs a stochastic dual simplex method to determine the optimal control parameters, while the second utilizes a genetic filter to refine the solution. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through simulations of a fixed-wing aircraft, where it successfully achieves steady, stable flight and precise landing.

We demonstrate that the scattering amplitude for this channel is governed by a single complex parameter, $a$, which encapsulates the essential low-energy dynamics. This parameter is defined as $a = \frac{1}{2}(\alpha + i\beta)$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ represent the real and imaginary components of the amplitude, respectively. The CMS Phase-1 Pixel Prototype Blade serves as a critical component of the CMS detector, designed to enhance the performance of the upgraded pixel system. This blade comprises 128 modules, each featuring 32 readout channels, and is engineered to withstand the extreme radiation environment of the CMS detector. The blade's design allows for the reconstruction of individual module data, enabling the analysis of readout performance and the identification of faulty channels. This study details the reconstruction software developed for the blade and presents the results of its application to CMS Phase-1 Pixel Prototype Blade data.

We have developed a machine learning framework to classify the morphologies of active galactic nucleus (AGN) host galaxies at redshifts $z < 1$ using the Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) survey. Leveraging a dataset of 1,000 AGN hosts from the HSC survey, we trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) to distinguish between disk and spheroid types. Our results indicate that the CNN achieves a classification accuracy of 90.5% for disk galaxies and 89.5% for spheroids. Furthermore, we employed the CNN to analyze the morphological evolution of AGN hosts across the redshift range $0 < z < 1$. Our findings reveal that the fraction of disk-type AGN hosts remains constant at approximately 60% throughout this epoch, whereas the fraction of spheroid-type AGN hosts increases from roughly 30% at $z=0.5$ to 40% at $z=0$.

This study examines the phase-space distribution of short-distance correlations within nuclei, specifically focusing on the interplay between the spatial and momentum domains. We demonstrate that the phase-space density of these correlations is not uniform; rather, it is concentrated in a specific region of phase space. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of the nuclear potential on the spatial distribution of these correlations.

This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to generate complex-valued representations of students, enabling the prediction of their future academic performance. The model utilizes complex-valued convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to process student data, which is organized into a two-dimensional matrix comprising a spatial dimension (representing the student's class) and a feature dimension (representing their attributes). The resulting complex-valued embeddings are subsequently mapped to a real-valued output space to predict future grades. The paper details the model's architecture, training methodology, and evaluation results, demonstrating that this approach achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This work examines the saturation regime of the gluon distribution within the proton, a phenomenon that arises from the nonlinear dynamics of the QCD evolution equations. We demonstrate that this saturation regime is characterized by geometric scaling, a property that has been confirmed by experimental data. Furthermore, we explore the implications of saturation for the saturation scale, $Q_s$, and its role in the context of heavy ion collisions.

The mass distribution of stars is a critical factor in determining the chemical evolution of the universe. While the initial mass function (IMF) is widely accepted as the primary driver of stellar mass distribution, recent findings suggest that the final mass distribution may also be influenced by the initial mass function (IMF) and the initial metallicity of the star. This study investigates the final mass distribution of low-metallicity stars, which are essential for understanding the chemical evolution of the early universe. We utilized the MESA stellar evolution code to simulate the evolution of low-metallicity stars, focusing on the final mass distribution of these objects. Our results indicate that the final mass distribution of low-metallicity stars is significantly affected by the initial mass function and the initial metallicity of the star. We also examined the relationship between the final mass distribution of low-metallicity stars and the initial mass function and the initial metallicity of the star. Our findings suggest that the final mass distribution of low-metallicity stars is significantly affected by the initial mass function and the initial metallicity of the star. We also examined the relationship between the final mass distribution of low-metallicity stars and the initial mass function and the initial metallicity of the star. Our findings suggest that the final mass distribution of low-metallicity stars is significantly affected by the initial mass function and the initial metallicity of the star. We also examined the relationship between the final mass distribution of low-metallicity stars and the initial mass function and the initial metallicity of the star.

This study introduces a novel toolbox designed to assess the sensitivity of machine learning forecasts, specifically targeting the financial literacy domain. The toolbox comprises three distinct modules: (1) a feature importance module that quantifies the impact of input variables on model predictions, (2) a feature interaction module that identifies how pairs of variables jointly influence forecasts, and (3) a feature perturbation module that measures the sensitivity of predictions to alterations in input data. The authors apply this toolbox to a unique dataset of 1,000 individuals, utilizing it to analyze the determinants of financial literacy. The results indicate that financial literacy is primarily driven by the interaction between gender and education levels, as well as the interaction between education levels and income. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that financial literacy exhibits high sensitivity to changes in income and education levels, whereas it remains relatively insensitive to variations in gender.

Quantum computing is a rapidly advancing field with significant potential to transform various sectors, including artificial intelligence, medicine, and finance. This paper introduces a novel quantum artificial neural network (QANN) designed to solve the XOR problem, a classic benchmark for evaluating machine learning algorithms. The proposed QANN integrates a quantum perceptron with a quantum support vector machine (QSVM). The quantum perceptron serves as the initial layer, utilizing a quantum circuit to process input data and generate a quantum state. Subsequently, the QSVM layer operates on this state to produce the final output. The study demonstrates that this hybrid QANN successfully resolves the XOR problem, achieving a 100% accuracy rate.

This paper introduces the concept of distorted product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds within nearly contact manifolds and examines their geometric characteristics. Furthermore, it investigates the geometric properties of the distorted product of pointwise inclined submanifolds.

We introduce a novel concept for detecting low-energy nuclear recoils using color centers in diamond, which are created by ionizing radiation. This method offers a highly sensitive, low-cost, and scalable approach to measuring such recoils. The proposed technique involves irradiating a diamond sample with neutrons, followed by scanning it with a laser to detect the resulting color centers. The study outlines the necessary conditions for this detection, including the required laser wavelength, the specific color centers to target, and the optimal diamond type. Additionally, we present a preliminary low-energy neutron sensitivity analysis for a 100 g diamond sample, demonstrating that the method could achieve a sensitivity of $10^{-10}$ neutrons/cm$^2$/s.

This study examines the dynamics of active colloidal particles within a two-dimensional activity gradient. We analyze the system's behavior across three distinct regimes: (i) a static regime where particles remain localized, (ii) a dynamic regime characterized by particle diffusion, and (iii) a mixed regime featuring coexisting localized and diffusive states. We demonstrate that the transition between the static and dynamic regimes is governed by the interplay between the activity gradient and the particles' self-propulsion speed. Furthermore, we show that the spatial distribution of particles in the mixed regime is dictated by the magnitude of the activity gradient.

We introduce a new theoretical framework for fractional quantum Hall systems that accounts for numerous magnetoroton branches, a phenomenon previously overlooked. This approach enables the calculation of the total energy spectrum for the system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spectral sum rules for the longitudinal and Hall conductivity are satisfied, a result that validates the consistency of our proposed model.

This study introduces a geometric approach to identify outbreak clusters within networks. The method relies on the concept of a "clustering radius," which represents the maximum distance between any two nodes within a specific group. By applying this metric, we can partition a network into distinct groups, each defined by a specific clustering radius. The algorithm operates by iteratively removing the node with the highest degree and assigning it to a new group, while simultaneously updating the clustering radius to maintain group integrity. The effectiveness of this technique is demonstrated through its application to real-world data, specifically the 2014 Ebola outbreak in West Africa.

This study examines the impact of X-shaped artifacts surrounding bright sources in maximum probability CMB maps, which are generated using the Hivemap algorithm. We demonstrate that these artifacts can be mitigated by applying a mask to the input data prior to map creation. Furthermore, we show that the mask's size is a critical parameter, as it directly influences the resulting map's fidelity.

Language-driven goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) has recently emerged as a promising approach for developing agents capable of executing complex tasks. However, a significant challenge remains: how to effectively represent goals using natural language. While prior research has largely focused on natural language processing (NLP) techniques to generate goal descriptions, this study investigates the impact of natural language on the learning process itself. We demonstrate that using natural language for goal representation can hinder learning due to referential uncertainty, where multiple valid descriptions exist for a single state. To address this, we introduce a novel method that mitigates referential uncertainty by incorporating a language model to generate diverse natural language goal descriptions. Our experiments show that this approach significantly improves sample efficiency and final performance.

Shadow tomography of quantum channels is a technique designed to efficiently estimate the properties of a quantum channel using a limited number of copies. This approach relies on the concept of "classical shadows," which are classical data structures capable of predicting various observables of a quantum state with high accuracy. In this work, we introduce a shadow method tailored for quantum channels, enabling the prediction of channel characteristics from classical shadows derived from the channel's input states. We demonstrate that this method is highly versatile, allowing for the estimation of diverse channel properties, including the average gate fidelity, the diamond norm distance, and the entanglement fidelity.

This paper establishes a sharp upper bound for the Cheeger constant of a two-dimensional convex domain, expressed as a function of its area. We further demonstrate that this bound is tight for both disks and rectangles.

This study addresses the challenge of optimizing a UAV's trajectory to maximize the total data collected from a set of ground targets within a fixed time frame. The UAV is equipped with a wireless communication link, and the data acquisition rate from each target is modeled as a function of the distance between the UAV and the target. The problem is formulated as a non-convex optimization task. To solve it, we propose a suboptimal algorithm based on successive convex approximation (SCA). Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing benchmarks.

We investigate the renormalization group evolution of the Coulomb interaction within a two-dimensional electron system confined to a bilayer graphene structure. Our analysis reveals that the interaction strength increases as the energy scale decreases, eventually diverging at a specific critical point. This instability arises from the interplay between the two-dimensional nature of the system and the Coulomb interaction, which is further amplified by the presence of a finite energy gap.

This study examines the thermal evolution of the conformation of Sc2TbN@C80 molecules adsorbed on a h-BN/Ni(111) substrate using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM). The findings reveal that the molecules initially adopt a C2v symmetry, which transitions to Ih symmetry upon heating to 300 K. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the C2v conformation is not an intrinsic property of the Sc2TbN@C80 molecule itself but rather a result of its interaction with the h-BN/Ni(111) surface.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, encompassing a vast array of devices that communicate via the Internet. These devices are typically characterized by limited computational power, restricted memory, and minimal energy reserves. Consequently, security protocols for IoT must be highly efficient to ensure the longevity of battery-powered hardware. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of lightweight cryptographic algorithms, evaluating their performance across computational speed, memory footprint, and energy consumption.

The Ramsey series technique is a standard method for measuring atomic and molecular properties, such as magnetic moments and electric dipole moments, with high precision. This study introduces a sequential Bayesian trial design for adaptive Ramsey series measurements, enabling the determination of optimal experimental parameters. We demonstrate that this approach can significantly enhance measurement precision by a factor of 1.5 to 2.0 compared to fixed-parameter strategies.

This study introduces a novel metric for assessing node centrality within complex networks, grounded in the concept of "importance" as defined by Gromov. We demonstrate that this Gromov-based measure effectively captures the structural significance of nodes, particularly in scenarios where traditional centrality metrics fail. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical framework for this importance, proving that it satisfies the axioms of a metric space.

This paper introduces a new theory of gravity, termed the Azimuthally Uniform Theory of Gravity (AUTG), which is built upon the principle of azimuthal uniformity. The theory's field equations are derived using the method of variation, and the resulting solutions are applied to investigate the dynamics of a test particle within a Schwarzschild-like metric.

This paper investigates the classification of collections of matrix pencils under stringent equivalence, a relation defined by the existence of a nonsingular matrix $S$ such that $A_i = S^{-1}A_iS$ for all $A_i$ in the set. We demonstrate that the stringent equivalence class of a collection is uniquely determined by the stringent equivalence class of its commutant. Furthermore, we establish that the commutant of a collection of matrix pencils is always a direct sum of commutative algebras, each of which is isomorphic to a direct sum of full matrix rings. Finally, we provide a complete classification of collections of matrix pencils up to stringent equivalence when the collection consists of a single pencil.

We establish a geometric T-duality framework for twisted tori, a class of spaces that includes both torus bundles and torus quotients. This approach relies on the concept of a twisted torus groupoid, which serves as a geometric model for the twisted torus.

We present a succinct representation of the shortest-path distance matrix for a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and treewidth $k$, requiring only $O(nk^2)$ bits. This approach is applicable to graphs with bounded treewidth, as well as those with bounded genus or excluding a fixed minor. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the distance matrix for graphs with treewidth $k$ can be encoded in $O(nk)$ bits, provided the graph is planar or excludes a fixed minor.

This paper examines discrete-interval dynamical systems defined by a continuous, strongly monotonic map $f: I \to I$ on a compact interval $I \subset \mathbb{R}$. We establish that such systems exhibit widespread chaotic behavior, specifically demonstrating that the $\omega$-limit set of almost every point is a Cantor set. Furthermore, we prove that the system possesses a dense orbit within the entire interval $I$.

Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are a prominent class of hybrid quantum-classical algorithms designed to solve optimization problems. However, their widespread adoption is hindered by the "barren plateau" phenomenon, which causes the cost landscape to become nearly flat, thereby impeding the convergence of the classical optimizer. This study introduces a novel adaptive strategy for VQAs that mitigates barren plateaus by dynamically adjusting the ansatz circuit based on the excitation count of the qubit system. We demonstrate that this approach significantly accelerates the convergence of the classical optimizer. Furthermore, we validate the method's efficacy by solving the ground state of the transverse-field Ising model, showing that it successfully avoids barren plateaus and achieves high accuracy.

Generative models have become a cornerstone of modern machine learning, serving as powerful tools for data representation and inference. This paper introduces a novel generative framework that employs a deep probabilistic model to capture the data distribution, utilizing a variational autoencoder (VAE) as its core. By applying a maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation approach to the latent variables, the model learns a more robust representation of the input data. This representation is then used to generate new samples that closely resemble the training distribution. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

The NANOGrav collaboration has recently reported compelling evidence for a stochastic gravitational-wave background (GWB) with a characteristic strain of $h_c \sim 10^{-25}$ at a frequency of $f \sim 10^{-8}$ Hz. This finding is consistent with a background generated by the amplification of primordial quantum fluctuations during inflation, a scenario that would also produce a GWB detectable by Advanced LIGO-Virgo (ALV) at frequencies around $10^{-2}$ Hz. We demonstrate that the amplitude of this background at ALV frequencies is directly proportional to the Hubble strain, $h_H$, which quantifies the fractional strain of the GWB at the Hubble scale. Consequently, the GWB amplitude at ALV frequencies is constrained by the Hubble tension, a discrepancy between early- and late-universe measurements of the Hubble constant. We further show that the Hubble strain is linked to the amplitude of the GWB at NANOGrav frequencies, thereby establishing a connection between the two. This relationship allows the GWB to serve as a probe of the Hubble tension, potentially offering a novel test of the accuracy cosmology framework.

This study presents the inaugural interferometric analysis of comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). The investigation focuses on the coma's spatial distribution of carbon monosulfide (CS) and carbon monoxide (CO) to determine their production rates and spatial scales. The findings reveal that the CS coma is significantly more extended than the CO coma, with a production rate of $1.1 \pm 0.2 \times 10^{27}$ molecules per second. This CS production rate is approximately 100 times greater than that of CO, which was measured at $1.1 \pm 0.2 \times 10^{25}$ molecules per second. The CS coma's spatial distribution is modeled using a two-component approach: a central, compact source and a distant, extended source. The compact component is located at a heliocentric distance of $1.1 \pm 0.1$ AU, while the extended component originates from $2.1 \pm 0.1$ AU. The study concludes that the CS coma likely arises from a combination of a central source and a distributed source, with the latter being the dominant contributor. This study introduces a straightforward and efficient method for generating speech from text without requiring any training data. The approach utilizes a pre-trained language model to generate phonemes and employs a pre-trained vocoder to synthesize audio from these phonemes. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art unsupervised speech generation techniques.

This study investigates the thermodynamic properties of a black hole within the context of holographic dark energy, employing a Tsallis holographic dark energy framework. The analysis focuses on the influence of quintessence, modeled as a scalar field with a complex-valued potential, on the system's thermodynamics. The findings indicate that the black hole's thermodynamic behavior is significantly contingent upon the parameters of the quintessence field. Furthermore, the study reveals that the black hole's entropy is not solely a function of its horizon area but also depends on the dark energy density.

This study introduces a novel hybrid algorithm designed to address Multi-Objective Mixed Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) challenges. The proposed method integrates the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) with a Branch and Bound (B&B) framework. Within this hybrid approach, the B&B component manages the integer variables, while NSGA-II optimizes the continuous variables. The algorithm's efficacy is validated through a case study involving the design of a multi-stage chemical reactor, which involves optimizing both integer and continuous variables. The results demonstrate that the hybrid algorithm outperforms the standard NSGA-II algorithm in terms of both solution quality and computational efficiency.

This paper demonstrates that within the framework of Synthetic Differential Geometry, any Lie groupoid possessing a Lie algebra that is linked to it is inherently connected and constitutes a Lie group.

The rapid advancement of biomedical research relies heavily on the exchange of large-scale datasets, which are often stored in diverse formats and locations. To address this, we have developed a Cyberinfrastructure Portal (CIP) designed to enable secure and efficient data sharing. This portal offers a unified interface for accessing data across various sources, supports multiple access methods, and ensures data security. We have successfully deployed this portal to facilitate the exchange of biomedical data, specifically for the National Cancer Institute's Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) project.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) aims to determine the sentiment polarity of a target entity within a specific aspect. While recent advancements have largely focused on modeling the relationship between aspects and targets, the critical role of the target entity itself remains underexplored. This study introduces a novel framework that explicitly models target sentiment by integrating a guided contrastive pre-training strategy. This approach enhances the target's representation through contrastive learning, utilizing a guidance mechanism to ensure the target's embedding aligns with its corresponding aspect. Furthermore, we propose a new target-centric pre-training task designed to capture the target's sentiment nuances. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on three major ABSD benchmarks.

This study introduces a novel method for analyzing mediation in case-control sampling, specifically addressing scenarios where the mediator is binary. The approach utilizes a two-stage regression framework to estimate direct and indirect effects, accounting for the case-control design. The authors establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of these estimators and provide a simulation study to evaluate the method's performance. Furthermore, the paper applies this methodology to a case-control dataset examining the role of obesity as a mediator in the relationship between physical activity and breast cancer risk.

This study investigates resilient transmission design for reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted secure multiuser communication systems, specifically addressing hardware imperfections in both the transmitter and the RIS. The primary objective is to maximize the weighted sum secrecy rate (WSSR) by optimizing the transmit beamforming vector, the passive reflection coefficients, and the active gain of the RIS. To mitigate the non-convexity of the optimization problem, we employ a successive convex approximation (SCA) approach. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of practical constraints, including the finite resolution of RIS elements and the limited active gain of the RIS. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves significant performance gains compared to conventional schemes, particularly under conditions of imperfect hardware.

This paper introduces a novel approach to resampling and renaming insights, termed Executive Function (EF). EF is a comparative value strategy that evaluates the worth of insights by contrasting them against one another. The study demonstrates that EF can be applied to resample and rename insights, and it is also used to summarize the results of hindsight analysis.

This study examines PSP's initial 10 orbits, which brought the spacecraft to a heliocentric distance of 0.13 AU. We analyze the energy flow within the solar wind by calculating the Poynting flux and the kinetic energy flux, alongside the magnetic helicity flux. We establish a general framework for constructing noncommutative countable principal bundles within the realm of noncommutative geometry. This approach extends the work of Rieffel, who originally defined such bundles through the action of a countable group on a unital C*-algebra. Our construction yields a noncommutative principal bundle equipped with a noncommutative structure group, a noncommutative base space, and a noncommutative total space. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the associated noncommutative principal bundle serves as a noncommutative generalization of a classical principal bundle.

This paper investigates the cardinal characteristics known as the ultrafilter and nearly disjointness values, denoted as $\mathfrak{v}$ and $\mathfrak{n}$, respectively. We demonstrate that $\mathfrak{n} \leq \mathfrak{v}$ and establish that the inequality $\mathfrak{n} < \mathfrak{v}$ is consistent with ZFC. Furthermore, we prove that $\mathfrak{v}$ is a regular limit cardinal and that the interval $[\mathfrak{n}, \mathfrak{v}]$ contains a stationary set of regular cardinals.

This study investigates the transmission and slowing of light within a $q$-deformed optomechanical system featuring a driven cavity and a two-level atom. We demonstrate that the transmission coefficient is governed by the deformation parameter $q$, which can be tuned to achieve either transparency or opacity. Furthermore, we analyze the group velocity of the transmitted light, revealing that it can be significantly reduced to the "slow" regime by adjusting the driving field intensity and the deformation parameter $q$.

The Double-Rotors Model (DRM) is a two-body framework that effectively describes the rotational spectra of odd-odd nuclei. This study examines the DRM's response to a specific type of perturbation, which is a two-body interaction acting between the two constituent rotors. This interaction is a component of the R-parity scissors mode, a collective excitation observed in odd-odd nuclei. The DRM's reaction to this perturbation is analyzed through the calculation of the corresponding energy shift and mixing angle. The results indicate that the DRM can account for the R-parity scissors mode, provided the two-body interaction is attractive.

This study introduces a neural network-based approach for solving both hyperbolic and elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs). The method employs a cell-mean formulation to define the loss function, which is then minimized using a backpropagation algorithm. The resulting neural network architecture is capable of approximating the solution to the PDE. The proposed technique is validated through several numerical examples, including the Poisson equation, the Helmholtz equation, the Laplace equation, the convection-diffusion equation, the wave equation, and the heat equation.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC is dedicated to investigating the properties of strongly interacting matter, specifically the quark-gluon plasma (QGP), which forms under extreme temperature and density conditions. This study outlines the ALICE upgrade designed to enhance the experiment's capabilities beyond the LHC Run 3 era. The upgraded setup will enable ALICE to probe a broader range of collision energies, including the upcoming High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) phase, and to analyze systems with varying degrees of strangeness. Furthermore, the experiment will expand its reach to study heavy-ion collisions involving lead, lead, and xenon nuclei, as well as proton-nucleus interactions.

We introduce a novel method for detecting the temporal Unruh effect, a phenomenon in which a uniformly accelerated observer perceives a vacuum state as a thermal bath. This detection relies on measuring the Berry phase acquired by a quantum system undergoing acceleration. Our findings indicate that the magnitude of this phase is directly proportional to the temperature of the thermal bath.

This paper introduces MEE, a novel dataset designed for occasion extraction, featuring 1,000 manually annotated examples across 10 languages. We also present a unique annotation scheme that captures the temporal and spatial details of occasions, including their start and end times, locations, and associated entities. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the dataset's characteristics and offer a detailed examination of the challenges involved in occasion extraction.

This paper investigates global vector bundles over a smooth manifold $M$ and their associated characteristic structures. We establish a positivity condition for these structures, which serves as a necessary requirement for a bundle to be globally realizable. Furthermore, we examine the push-forward of vector bundles from a submanifold $N$ into $M$, deriving a positivity condition for the resulting characteristic structure on $M$. This condition is also necessary for the existence of such a push-forward. Finally, we demonstrate that the push-forward of a globally realizable bundle remains globally realizable.

We present a study of the hard spectral state of the black hole binary Cyg X-1, utilizing data from the NICER mission. Our analysis reveals that the hard X-ray emission is modulated by a low-frequency quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) with a frequency of approximately 0.1 Hz. This modulation is characterized by a variable amplitude and a spectral shape that evolves over time. We interpret this behavior as a stellar breeze, a phenomenon where the stellar wind from the companion star impacts the black hole's accretion flow. This stellar breeze is proposed to be the origin of the observed low-frequency QPO.

We introduce a non-Abelian extension of the aether-similar term found in the Standard Model Extension (SME), which is a framework for Lorentz violation. This term is a Lorentz-violating, dimension-three operator that breaks Lorentz symmetry in a way analogous to the Standard Model's Higgs mechanism. We demonstrate that this new operator can be integrated into the Standard Model, and we analyze its effects on the Higgs boson's mass and the resulting symmetry breaking. Furthermore, we examine the operator's behavior at finite temperature, showing that it can induce a phase transition in the early universe. Finally, we discuss potential experimental signatures of this Lorentz-violating term.

This paper introduces a collaborative framework for syntactic and semantic analysis, designed to overcome the limitations of traditional methods that rely on syntactic parsing alone. By integrating syntactic and semantic information, the proposed approach enhances the accuracy of semantic analysis. The study details the collaborative architecture, the specific algorithms employed, and the results of experiments conducted on the Chinese Universal Syntactic and Semantic Analysis (CUSSA) dataset.

We investigate the influence of disk magnetic fields on the postmerger evolution of neutrino-cooled accretion disks, utilizing a 3D general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) framework. Our simulations reveal that magnetic fields can drive significant mass ejection, with the most extreme cases ejecting up to 0.001 solar masses. This ejected mass is predominantly expelled along the disk's rotational axis, forming a bipolar outflow. Furthermore, we demonstrate that magnetic fields can generate a substantial jet, with the most intense scenarios producing a jet power of approximately 10^50 erg/s.

We present a study of the tidal features surrounding 100 massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) with stellar masses exceeding $10^{11} M_{\odot}$, identified in the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). Utilizing the HSC-SSP public data, we analyzed the flux distribution of tidal tails and shells across the $g$ and $i$ bands. Our findings indicate that the flux fraction of tidal shells and tails is roughly 10% of the total galaxy flux, a value consistent with previous studies of ETGs in the local universe. Furthermore, we calculated the merger rate for these galaxies by examining the flux fraction of tidal features. The results reveal that the merger rate for these massive ETGs is approximately $10^{-2}$ Gyr$^{-1}$, a figure comparable to those observed in lower-mass ETGs and spiral galaxies.

We present a new method for analyzing the optical counterparts of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) by utilizing the precise timing of radio bursts to establish strict upper limits on the optical emission. This approach is applicable to both simultaneous and delayed optical signals. We demonstrate that this technique can significantly lower the upper limits on optical emission for FRBs, thereby enhancing the sensitivity of future optical surveys.

While language models excel at generating text, they often lack the ability to incorporate external information, such as visual inputs, into their output. This study introduces a new framework for text generation that integrates visual controls, enabling models to produce content conditioned on specific visual cues. We demonstrate that this approach allows for the creation of text describing images, generating image captions, and creating text for images with specific attributes. Our findings indicate that models trained with visual controls achieve superior performance in these tasks compared to those relying solely on text data.

RingCT serves as the cryptographic foundation for the Monero blockchain, enabling anonymous transactions through the use of ring signatures and Pedersen commitments. While RingCT offers superior privacy and efficiency compared to its predecessor, it remains vulnerable to a specific attack vector: the inclusion of fake transactions within the blockchain. This vulnerability arises because the protocol lacks a mechanism to verify that a transaction is not fabricated. To address this, we introduce a novel delegation scheme that allows a transaction to be verified by a single, randomly selected participant from the ring. This approach ensures that the probability of a fake transaction remaining undetected is negligible, while simultaneously preserving the anonymity of the actual sender.

This paper details the methodology and outcomes of a brightness scan performed on the Cornell Electron Storage Ring (CESR) utilizing the Cornell High Energy Synchrotron Source (CHESS) U11 beamline. The brightness scan serves as a diagnostic tool for characterizing the electron beam's properties. The study presents the brightness measurements recorded at the U11 beamline, which were derived from the measured horizontal and vertical spectra of the photon beam. The brightness scan was conducted by varying the horizontal and vertical beam sizes, which were adjusted using the horizontal and vertical beam position monitors (BPMs) and the horizontal and vertical beam size monitors (BSMs).
